# Lab 5 — SAST and DAST: Reading the Code, Then Watching It Run

## Task 1 — DAST, twice

I ran ZAP twice against Juice Shop. First I ran the unauthenticated baseline scan, which is mostly passive. After that I ran the authenticated scan using `labs/lab5/scripts/zap-auth.yaml`, which logs in and also performs active tests.

| Scan | Scan time | High | Medium | Low | Informational | Total alert types | Unique URLs with findings |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Unauthenticated baseline | Approximately 2 minutes; exact elapsed time was not separately recorded | 0 | 2 | 5 | 3 | 10 | 13 |
| Authenticated active scan | 12m 32s | 2 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 13 | 21 |

**Evidence — unauthenticated baseline run.**

<img alt="Task 1 evidence showing the unauthenticated ZAP baseline scan run." src="data:image/png;base64," />

**Evidence — unauthenticated baseline counts.**

<img alt="Task 1 evidence showing unauthenticated baseline alert counts." src="data:image/png;base64," />

**Evidence — side-by-side scan comparison.**

<img alt="Task 1 evidence comparing authenticated and unauthenticated ZAP scans." src="data:image/png;base64," />

The authenticated scan found more alert types: **13** instead of **10**. The bigger difference is the severity: the baseline scan only reached **Medium**, while the authenticated active scan found **two High-risk alerts**.

The two High-risk findings were:

| Alert | Risk / confidence | URL or endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| SQL Injection | High / Low confidence | `GET /rest/products/search?q=%27%28` and `POST /rest/user/login` |
| Vulnerable JS Library | High / Medium confidence | `GET /chunk-GJJPXCX3.js` |

For the SQL Injection alert, ZAP changed the `q` and `email` parameters using SQL-related characters and got `HTTP 500 Internal Server Error` responses. Since the confidence was Low, I would not treat this as final proof of SQL injection yet. I would treat it as something important to validate manually.

**Evidence — High-risk authenticated findings.**

<img alt="Task 1 evidence showing high-risk findings from the authenticated active scan." src="data:image/png;base64," />

### Authenticated-only alerts

Some alert types appeared only in the authenticated active report. Examples include `SQL Injection`, `Vulnerable JS Library`, `Session ID in URL Rewrite`, `Private IP Disclosure`, and `Missing Anti-clickjacking Header`.

But this does not automatically mean that all those URLs require login. I manually checked that `/rest/admin/application-configuration` returned `HTTP 200 OK` without credentials. An anonymous request could also create a new Socket.IO session. So, in this run, the difference was mostly caused by better crawl coverage and by the active scan phase, not only by authenticated-only pages.

Two examples:

| Authenticated-only alert | URL | Why it did not appear in the baseline |
|---|---|---|
| SQL Injection | `/rest/products/search?q=%27%28` and `/rest/user/login` | These endpoints can be reached anonymously, but the baseline scan is passive. It does not send SQL injection payloads. The authenticated scan includes active testing, so it changed parameters and found abnormal server responses. |
| Private IP Disclosure | `/rest/admin/application-configuration` | I confirmed that this endpoint can be reached anonymously. So this finding appeared only in the authenticated report because of scan coverage, not because authentication was required. |

### Why alert count alone is a poor comparison

The number of alerts alone is a bad comparison because **13 versus 10** looks like a small difference, but the authenticated scan found two High-risk issues while the baseline found none. I would report the severity, confidence, affected URLs, and whether the findings are reproducible, not only the total count. This means a pipeline that only runs `zap-baseline.py` against staging is useful as a passive baseline check, but it is not full DAST coverage. It can miss issues that require active payloads or authenticated application flows.

## Task 2 — SAST on the same version

Semgrep was run against the Juice Shop `v20.0.0` source code, which matches the container version scanned by ZAP.

| Severity | Count |
|---|---:|
| ERROR | 13 |
| WARNING | 14 |
| **Total** | **27** |

The most common rules were:

| Count | Rule |
|---:|---|
| 6 | `javascript.sequelize.security.audit.sequelize-injection-express.express-sequelize-injection` |
| 5 | `yaml.github-actions.security.run-shell-injection.run-shell-injection` |
| 4 | `javascript.express.security.audit.express-check-directory-listing.express-check-directory-listing` |
| 4 | `javascript.express.security.audit.express-res-sendfile.express-res-sendfile` |
| 4 | `yaml.github-actions.security.github-actions-mutable-action-tag.github-actions-mutable-action-tag` |
| 1 | `javascript.express.security.audit.express-open-redirect.express-open-redirect` |
| 1 | `javascript.jsonwebtoken.security.jwt-hardcode.hardcoded-jwt-secret` |
| 1 | `javascript.lang.security.audit.code-string-concat.code-string-concat` |
| 1 | `yaml.github-actions.security.gha-curl-pipe-shell.gha-curl-pipe-shell` |

Semgrep reported **57 errors**. Most of them were parse errors in the isolated teaching snippets under `data/static/codefixes/` or timeouts while scanning some translation JSON files. The lab says parse errors and timeouts are expected here, so I do not treat this as invalidating the scan.

**Evidence — Semgrep severity, rules, and error count.**

<img alt="Task 2 evidence showing Semgrep severity split, top rules, and error count." src="data:image/png;base64," />

One workflow finding was `yaml.github-actions.security.github-actions-mutable-action-tag.github-actions-mutable-action-tag`, for example at `.github/workflows/ci.yml:202`. This connects to Lecture 4 because GitHub Actions are part of the CI/CD supply chain. If an action is referenced by a mutable tag instead of a commit SHA, the pipeline can run different upstream code later without the repository changing.

I would suppress the `express-check-directory-listing` finding at `server.ts:273` as a false positive. The flagged code serves `/.well-known` as public static content:

```ts
app.use('/.well-known', serveIndexMiddleware, serveIndex('.well-known', { icons: true, view: 'details' }))
app.use('/.well-known', express.static('.well-known'))
```

The rule is normally useful because directory listing can expose files by accident. In this case, `.well-known` is meant to be public metadata, such as `/.well-known/csaf/provider-metadata.json`, so I would not treat this specific finding as an accidental internal directory exposure.

If I could fix one rule first, I would choose `express-sequelize-injection`. Semgrep found unsafe Sequelize query patterns in real routes such as `routes/login.ts:34` and `routes/search.ts:23`. This is the most important rule to prioritize because ZAP also reported SQL Injection behavior against `/rest/user/login` and `/rest/products/search`. I would replace string-built SQL with parameterized queries or prepared statements.

## Bonus — One bug, two tools

| OWASP category | ZAP alert and URL | Semgrep rule and source |
|---|---|---|
| A05:2025 — Injection | `SQL Injection` → `GET /rest/products/search?q=%27%28` | `express-sequelize-injection` → `routes/search.ts:23` |

The strongest correlation is the product search endpoint. Semgrep found this code at `routes/search.ts:23`:

```ts
let criteria: any = req.query.q === 'undefined' ? '' : req.query.q ?? ''
criteria = (criteria.length <= 200) ? criteria : criteria.substring(0, 200)

models.sequelize.query(
  `SELECT * FROM Products WHERE ((name LIKE '%${criteria}%' OR description LIKE '%${criteria}%') AND deletedAt IS NULL) ORDER BY name`
)
```

The value from `req.query.q` is copied into `criteria` and then inserted directly into the SQL string. This means user-controlled input can change the SQL query.

ZAP tested the same endpoint with this request:

```text
GET /rest/products/search?q=%27%28
```

The decoded `q` value was:

```text
'(
```

ZAP observed:

```text
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
```

ZAP reported this as a High-risk SQL Injection alert. The ZAP confidence was Low, so I would still validate it manually, but the Semgrep result supports the same issue from the source code side.

A fix would be to use a parameterized query instead of building SQL with string interpolation:

```ts
models.sequelize.query(
  `SELECT * FROM Products
   WHERE ((name LIKE $criteria OR description LIKE $criteria)
   AND deletedAt IS NULL)
   ORDER BY name`,
  {
    bind: {
      criteria: `%${criteria}%`
    }
  }
)
```

This keeps the SQL structure separate from the user input, so special characters in the search term are treated as data.

I would put this SQL injection finding first in the PR description because both tools point to the same behavior. Semgrep shows the unsafe query in the code, and ZAP shows an abnormal runtime response when the endpoint is tested.
